problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{\text{i}\omega t}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).$$\,L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that the cosine function can be defined in terms of complex exponentials as follows: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)=\frac{{e}^{4\text{i}t}+{e}^{-4\text{i}t}}{2}
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{4\text{i}t}+{e}^{-4\text{i}t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{4\text{i}t}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{-4\text{i}t}}{2}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{4\text{i}t}}{2}}+L{\frac{{e}^{-4\text{i}t}}{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{4\text{i}t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-4\text{i}t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{\text{i}\omega t}}=\frac{1}{s-\text{i}\omega },\,s>0.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{4\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}},\,s>0 \\ L{{e}^{-4\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s+4\text{i}},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)} & =\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{4\text{i}t}}+\frac{1}{2}L{{e}^{-4\text{i}t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{s+4\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{s-4\text{i}}+\frac{1}{s+4\text{i}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{(s+4\text{i})+(s-4\text{i})}{(s-4\text{i})(s+4\text{i})}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{2s}{{s}^{2}+16}) \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+16},\end{aligned}
$$

defined for $s>0.$
